summary: Shapiro et al. 2011 provides the theoretical grounding for the persistence and concurrent-update semantics of the question/answer substrate. The paper distinguishes state-based CRDTs (CvRDTs), where replicas merge full states via a least-upper-bound (LUB) operation over a monotonic semilattice, from operation-based CRDTs (CmRDTs), where replicas apply effect-updates that commute. Strong Eventual Consistency (SEC) demands that correct replicas that have delivered the same updates have equivalent state, without requiring rollback or consensus. Sufficient conditions for SEC are monotonicity in a semilattice (CvRDT) and commutativity of concurrent updates (CmRDT). Reusable concrete types include the add-only (grow-only) set, the U-Set (observed-remove set using tombstones — actually presented as add-only A plus tombstone R), the increment/decrement counter, and a directed-graph CRDT. Design inferences for the question/answer substrate: model questions, answers, and tags as add-only sets (or add-wins sets for tags) so that concurrent additions converge; derive a directed-graph-like structure for question-answer-answer links; and identify invariants CRDTs cannot enforce — uniqueness of canonical object IDs, schema validity, and tag-vocabulary control — which the runtime must enforce.
unresolved: The paper does not specify how to choose between add-wins and remove-wins semantics for sets; the choice must be made per use case (the paper notes multiple alternatives are possible).
The paper's graph CRDT example is op-based and relies on a causal, reliable broadcast; the substrate's communication layer must provide this to use the graph directly.
The paper's garbage-collection algorithm for logs is only live if no process is crashed; the substrate must define its own tombstone or GC policy for removed elements.
The paper does not address how to compose CRDTs with runtime-enforced invariants without breaking the monotonicity or commutativity conditions.
